definition: Extrapolate means to extend known information beyond its last point to estimate what is unknown.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word extrapolate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know extrapolate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Census planners extrapolate a county's population from the handful of blocks they can actually visit.
To infer is milder than to extrapolate: an inference rests directly on the evidence in front of you, while extrapolation stretches that evidence out past its edge.
Conjecture goes further than extrapolate — it leaps with hardly any data at all, where extrapolation at least follows a measured trend.

Project runs current numbers forward — the business-page cousin of extrapolate. A treasurer projects next quarter's revenue from this quarter's books. Extrapolate is the broader, more technical move: extending any measured trend past its last data point, whether the data is money, votes, or rainfall.

Forecast predicts what is coming, in weather-report register — a forecast of storms, of turnout, of demand. It names the prediction, not the method. Extrapolate names the method itself: stretch the trend you measured past its final point and read off where it lands.

In 1954, plenty of physiologists insisted the four-minute mile sat at the very edge of human ability.
A statistician saw it differently.
Record times had been falling by nearly a second a year for three decades, and he simply let the line keep going.
To extrapolate from the trend was not to promise anything -- it was to say that if the curve held, a 3:58 would arrive within a few years.
The method has famous failures too.
Stretch the same line far enough and it predicts a two-minute mile, which no amount of training will ever deliver.
The lesson runners' statisticians repeat: data earns you the next step past its edge, and no more.
The farther beyond your last measurement you reach, the thinner the ground.
